title: Henry's break
hook: a king's divorce, a split from Rome, and monasteries dissolved

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tyndale's prayer at the stake. Your line was open the king's eyes.

A king wants a son. The story ends with empty monasteries. Henry the Eighth is married to Catherine of Aragon. She was first married to his older brother, Arthur, who died. Henry and Catherine have a daughter, Mary, but no son who lives. Henry becomes convinced the marriage was wrong from the very beginning, and asks the pope to declare it never truly existed. The pope does not give him the answer he wants. So Henry stops asking.
screen: `HE ASKS THE POPE TO END HIS MARRIAGE.`

segments.voice: Henry built his case on a verse. Leviticus says, in the King James Bible, "if a man shall take his brother's wife, it is an unclean thing", and adds that such a couple will be childless. His opponents pointed to Deuteronomy, which tells a man to marry his brother's widow if the brother died without children. Same Bible, two answers, and a crown between them. When Rome would not grant it, Henry and his Parliament cut the ties. Henry married Anne Boleyn in secret, and Thomas Cranmer, the new archbishop of Canterbury, declared the marriage to Catherine void. New laws named the king supreme head of the church in England. Then came the monasteries. Royal commissioners visited the abbeys and priories and reported on them, and one by one they were closed. Their lands went to the crown, and much was sold on to wealthy families. Monks and nuns who had given their lives to those houses were sent out. Some got pensions, some became parish priests, some had nowhere obvious to go. Roofs were stripped for their lead, and walls became quarries. The strange part: Henry did not think of himself as a Protestant. He kept the Mass. The break was first about authority, who rules the church in England. Anglicans trace their church's story through these years, though much of what shaped it came later. Catholics remember the break as a wound, and the closing of the monasteries as a loss. Faith and politics knot tightly here. Asked about taxes, Jesus said: "Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's." The hard question was who got to decide which was which.
screen: `THE KING AS HEAD OF THE CHURCH.`

segments.voice: Picture a monk or a nun walking out through an abbey gate for the last time, leaving a place they had meant to stay in for life. Then widen the picture to anyone today who has lost a home through decisions made far above them. If you pray, pray for them, then and now; if you don't, keep them company a while.
Henry's break. A king's quarrel over a marriage that became a split between the church in England and Rome, and the closing of England's monasteries.
Your line: politics and faith. When they tangle, ordinary people often pay the price. Day eight hundred sixty-seven.
